[[File:Michel Therrien.jpg|right|thumb|Michel Therrien was the Penguins' head coach from 2005 to 2009.]]

The [[Pittsburgh Penguins]] are an American professional [[ice hockey]] team based in [[Pittsburgh|Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]]. They play in the [[Metropolitan Division]] of the [[Eastern Conference (NHL)|Eastern Conference]] in the [[National Hockey League]] (NHL). The franchise was established as one of six new franchises of the [[1967 NHL expansion]].<ref>{{cite book |title= Professional Sports Team Histories: Hockey |last= Cooper|first= Bruce C.|editor= Michael L. LaBlanc|year= 1994|publisher= [[Gale (Cengage)|Gale Research Inc]]|page=322|location= [[Detroit|Detroit, Michigan]]|isbn= 978-0-8103-8862-8}}</ref> Since their foundation, the Penguins had played their home games at the [[Civic Arena (Pittsburgh)|Civic Arena]], which was replaced by the [[Consol Energy Center]] in [[2010-11 NHL season|2010]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://penguins.nhl.com/arena/index.htm |title=Consol Energy Center |access-date=6 January 2009 |publisher=PittsburghPenguins.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080822023358/http://penguins.nhl.com/arena/index.htm |archive-date=22 August 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The franchise is co-owned by [[Ronald Burkle]] and [[Mario Lemieux]]—the only player/owner in the NHL's modern era.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://penguins.nhl.com/team/app/?service=page&page=NHLPage&bcid=tea_office|title=Front Office|access-date=6 January 2009|work=Executive Staff|publisher=PittsburghPenguins.com|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081217092640/http://penguins.nhl.com/team/app/?service=page&page=NHLPage&bcid=tea_office|archive-date=17 December 2008}}</ref> According to [[Forbes]], the Penguins were the 11th most valuable NHL franchise, at [[United States dollar|US$]]222&nbsp;million, in 2009.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=NHL Team Valuations |url=https://www.forbes.com/lists/2009/31/hockey-values-09_NHL-Team-Valuations_Rank.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091114060632/http://www.forbes.com/lists/2009/31/hockey-values-09_NHL-Team-Valuations_Rank.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=November 14, 2009 |magazine=Forbes.com |date=2009-11-11 |access-date=2010-06-12}}</ref>

There have been 23&nbsp;[[Coach (ice hockey)|head coaches]] for the Penguins franchise.<ref name=OffSit>{{Cite web|url=http://penguins.nhl.com/team/app/?service=page&page=NHLPage&bcid=his_managers |title=General Managers and Coaches |access-date=30 December 2008 |work=Coaches |publisher=PittsburghPenguins.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090608115435/http://penguins.nhl.com/team/app/?service=page&page=NHLPage&bcid=his_managers |archive-date=8 June 2009 }}</ref> The franchise's first head coach was [[George Sullivan (ice hockey)|Red Sullivan]], former [[New York Rangers]] captain and coach.<ref>{{cite book |title=Penguin Profiles|last= O'Brien|first= Jim|year=1994|publisher=James P. O'Brien - Publishing|location=[[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]]|isbn=0-916114-16-3|pages=242–44}}</ref> Sullivan was replaced by future [[Hockey Hall of Fame]] inductee [[Red Kelly]], after two seasons. Kelly was inducted into the Hall of Fame as a player,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/players/k/kellyre01.html|title=Red Kelly Playing Record|access-date=2008-12-27|publisher=Sports Reference, LLC|work=Hockey-Reference.com|archive-date=2013-09-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130928180721/http://www.hockey-reference.com/players/k/kellyre01.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and head coaches [[Craig Patrick]], [[Bob Johnson (ice hockey, born 1931)|Bob Johnson]], [[Scotty Bowman]], and [[Herb Brooks]] were inducted as [[List of members of the Hockey Hall of Fame#Builders|builders]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legendsofhockey.net:8080/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/LegendsMembersByYear.jsp?type=Builder|title=Builders|access-date=2008-12-27|publisher=Hockey Hall of Fame|work=The Legends|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090528120538/http://www.legendsofhockey.net:8080/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/LegendsMembersByYear.jsp?type=Builder|archive-date=2009-05-28}}</ref> Bob Johnson led the Penguins to their first [[Stanley Cup]] victory in 1991, but was forced to retire due to health problems after the season—he died later that year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legendsofhockey.net:8080/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/LegendsMember.jsp?mem=b199202&type=Builder&page=bio&list=ByYear#photo|title=Bob Johnson Biography|access-date=30 December 2008|work=The Legends|publisher=Hockey Hall of Fame|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040529150900/http://www.legendsofhockey.net:8080/LegendsOfHockey/jsp/LegendsMember.jsp?mem=B199202#photo|archive-date=29 May 2004}}</ref> Bowman succeeded Johnson and coached the team to its second Stanley Cup victory the following season. [[Michel Therrien]] won the [[Prince of Wales Trophy]], as Eastern Conference champion, during the [[2007–08 NHL season|2007–08 season]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Eastern Finals: Game Five recap |url=http://penguins.nhl.com/team/app?gameNumber=315&gameType=3&page=Recap&season=20072008&service=page |agency=Associated Press |publisher=Pittsburgh Penguins |access-date=September 29, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080521040039/http://penguins.nhl.com/team/app?gameNumber=315&gameType=3&page=Recap&season=20072008&service=page |archive-date=May 21, 2008 }}</ref> Therrien was replaced the following season by [[Dan Bylsma]].<ref name=Blysma>{{cite news|first=Dave|last=Molinari|title=Therrien fired, Blysma in as Penguins' interim head coach|url=http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/09046/949415-100.stm|newspaper=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|date=15 February 2009|access-date=15 February 2009|archive-date=17 February 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090217233702/http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/09046/949415-100.stm|url-status=dead}}</ref> Bylsma would lead the Penguins to their third Stanley Cup championship that same season. Bylsma was fired after the 2013–14 season and replaced by Mike Johnston.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nhl/story/_/id/11132465/pittsburgh-penguins-hire-mike-johnston-coach|title=Penguins pluck WHL's Johnston to be coach|website=ESPN.com|date=June 25, 2014 |access-date=2016-06-13|archive-date=2016-06-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160617114814/http://espn.go.com/nhl/story/_/id/11132465/pittsburgh-penguins-hire-mike-johnston-coach|url-status=live}}</ref> Johnston was fired during the 2015–16 season and replaced by Mike Sullivan,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://penguins.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=792317|title=Mike Sullivan Named Head Coach of Pittsburgh Penguins|website=penguins.nhl.com|access-date=2016-06-13|archive-date=2015-12-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151215004716/http://penguins.nhl.com/club/news.htm?id=792317|url-status=dead}}</ref> who led the Penguins to consecutive Stanley Cup championships in 2016 and 2017 and leads the team in games coached. Sullivan ultimately departed the Penguins on April 28, 2025, following three consecutive seasons without a playoff appearance.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 28, 2025 |title=Penguins and Head Coach Mike Sullivan Agree to Part Ways |url=https://www.nhl.com/penguins/news/penguins-and-head-coach-mike-sullivan-agree-to-part-ways |access-date=April 28, 2025 |website=www.nhl.com}}</ref> [[Dan Muse]] was hired on June 4, 2025, succeeding Sullivan.<ref name="MuseHired" />

==Notes==
* {{note label|Note1|a|a}} Beginning with the 2005–06 season, the NHL instituted a [[Overtime (ice hockey)#Shootout|shootout]] for regular season games that remained tied after a five-minute overtime period, which prevented ties.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nhl.com/ext/0708rules.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080511234846/http://www.nhl.com/ext/0708rules.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=2008-05-11|title=Official Rules|publisher=Lincoln Hockey and the National Hockey League|work=NHL.com|access-date=2008-12-21}}</ref>
* {{note label|Note2|b|b}} Head coaches with multiple terms are counted once; figures are career totals. For a specific order of the coaches see the [[#Footnotes|Footnotes]] section.
* {{note label|Note3|c|c}} Each year is linked to an article about that particular NHL season. 
* {{note label|Note4|d|d}} Gene Ubriaco served as the Penguins' head coach to begin the 1989–90 season; the team began with a 10–14–2 record.<ref name=Pens198990>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/teams/PIT/1990.html|title=1989-90 Pittsburgh Penguins|access-date=6 January 2009|work=Hockey-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference, LLC.|archive-date=11 October 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081011094422/http://www.hockey-reference.com/teams/PIT/1990.html|url-status=live}}</ref> On December 5, 1989, Craig Patrick replaced Ubriaco as an interim head coach.<ref name=OffSit/><ref name=PatInt/> Under Patrick, the team went 22–26–6 and did not qualify for the playoffs.<ref name=Pens198990/>
* {{note label|Note5|e|e}} After starting the 1996–97 season with a record of 31–26–5,<ref name=Pens199697>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hockey-reference.com/teams/PIT/1997.html|title=1996-97 Pittsburgh Penguins|access-date=6 January 2009|work=Hockey-Reference.com|publisher=Sports Reference, LLC.|archive-date=21 August 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080821214618/http://www.hockey-reference.com/teams/PIT/1997.html|url-status=live}}</ref> the Penguins went 1–8 in nine consecutive games in February and March 1997.<ref name=PatInt>{{cite news |title= Penguins' Fire Johnston; Patrick Is Interim Coach |url= https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E03E4D81730F937A35750C0A961958260|newspaper= [[The New York Times]]|date= 4 March 1997|access-date=6 January 2009}}</ref> Coach Eddie Johnston was replaced by Craig Patrick, under whom the team finished the season 7–10–3 and lost in the first round of the playoffs four games to one.<ref name=Pens199697/>
* {{note label|Note6|f|f}} Michel Therrien coached the Penguins to a 27–25–5 record to start the 2008–09 season, at which point he was replaced by Dan Bylsma.<ref name=Blysma/>
* {{note label|Note7|g|g}} Mike Johnston coached the Penguins to a 15–10–3 record to start the 2015–16 season, at which point he was replaced by Mike Sullivan.<ref name=2015Coach/>
